name: Acetabular labral tear
populations: women with hip dysplasia or hypermobility
athletes in pivoting, kicking and end-range sports
summary: Detachment or splitting of the fibrocartilaginous rim of the hip socket, usually anterosuperior, causing groin pain and clicking. Often secondary to FAI morphology or dysplasia and common without symptoms.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: At least 3 months of exercise-based care; 4–9 months after arthroscopic repair

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: FADIR: high sensitivity, poor specificity; a negative test helps rule out intra-articular pain

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: 3 T MRI or MR arthrography (Sn ≈0.80–0.89, Sp ≈0.69–0.77)

keyFacts.label: Site
keyFacts.value: Anterosuperior quadrant in about three-quarters of tears

keyFacts.label: Caution
keyFacts.value: Labral tears are seen on MRI in about half of people without hip pain

keyFacts.label: Diagnostic delay
keyFacts.value: Mean 21 months from symptom onset in one surgical series

keywords.mechanism: Most labral tears result from repetitive loading of the anterosuperior rim: in FAI the femoral head–neck junction shears or crushes the labrum in flexion and internal rotation; in dysplasia the labrum is overloaded as the femoral head translates toward the shallow rim [r7]. An acute tear typically occurs during a forceful twist or pivot on a loaded, flexed hip, a slip into hyperabduction, or end-range hip extension with external rotation, which increases anterior joint force [r8].

name: Acute adductor longus strain
summary: An acute tear of the adductor longus at its proximal tendon, musculotendinous junction or pubic insertion, caused by rapid activation while the muscle is being rapidly lengthened in kicking or change of direction.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Median ~18 days to full training for MRI grade 0–2; ~11 weeks for complete tears/avulsions

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; being clinically pain-free before return is linked to fewer reinjuries

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Palpation of the proximal adductor longus plus resisted adduction (squeeze) reproducing the injury pain

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI only if a complete tear/avulsion is suspected or for prognosis in elite sport

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Young adults (median 27 years in an MRI cohort)

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: ~70% non-contact: change of direction, kicking, reaching, jumping

grading: MRI grading 0–3 (used in the Aspetar adductor cohort studies)

structures: Proximal adductor longus tendon and pubic enthesis
Adductor brevis, pectineus and obturator externus
Adductor longus MTJs (proximal or distal tendon)
Proximal adductor longus tendon / pubic enthesis
differentials: Hip-related groin pain (FAI syndrome / labral tear)
keywords.mechanism: Video analysis of acute adductor longus injuries in professional football found that 71% were non-contact and that more than half followed a quick reaction to a change in play [r4]. The injuring actions were change of direction (35%), kicking (29%), reaching (24%) and jumping (12%). Closed-chain injuries (change of direction, reaching) occurred with the hip extended, abducted and externally rotated. Open-chain injuries (kicking, jumping) occurred as the hip moved from extension to flexion and from abduction to adduction [r4]. The common thread is rapid muscle activation during rapid lengthening. In a maximal kick the adductor longus is lengthening fastest (~22 cm/s) near peak hip extension at about 40% of swing, just as it is activating to drive the limb forward [r5].

name: Acute hamstring strain
populations: older athletes with a previous hamstring injury
summary: A tear of the hamstring muscle fibres, usually the biceps femoris long head near its proximal musculotendinous junction, during high-speed running or an extreme hip-flexion stretch.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Sprint-type 2–8 weeks; stretch-type or intratendinous injuries take much longer

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based: pain-free palpation, strength, flexibility and maximal sprinting

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Palpation (site and length of tenderness) plus resisted knee flexion; Askling H-test before RTS

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not routine. MRI if avulsion is suspected, in elite athletes, or for recurrent injury

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 22% of elite male footballers per season

keyFacts.label: Recurrence
keyFacts.value: 13.9–63.3% within 2 years

keywords.mechanism: Sprint-type HSI occurs at maximal running speed, most often in late swing. The hip is flexed and the knee extends rapidly as the shank swings forward. The biarticular hamstrings contract eccentrically to decelerate the shank, so they are long, highly active and lengthening at their peak velocity [r10]. The long head of biceps femoris fails, typically near its proximal musculotendinous junction (MTJ) [r2]. Stretch-type HSI happens during slow, extreme hip flexion with the knee extended and usually affects the proximal semimembranosus tendon [r3].

name: Adductor-related groin pain (longstanding)
summary: Longstanding groin pain from the adductor longus origin (adductor tenderness plus pain on resisted adduction) that builds up in kicking and cutting sports and responds to progressive adductor strengthening.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: 8–12 weeks of progressive active training, then graded return

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: 79% returned to the same level without groin pain after active training

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Adductor longus origin palpation + resisted adduction (squeeze) reproducing pain

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Rarely needed. MRI changes are common in asymptomatic footballers

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Most common groin entity: 61% of athletes in a groin clinic

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Cumulative kicking, cutting and skating load exceeding adductor capacity

structures: Adductor longus enthesis and proximal tendon
differentials: Hip-related groin pain (FAI syndrome / labral tear)
Obturator nerve entrapment / referred lumbar pain
keywords.mechanism: ARGP develops when the cumulative load at the adductor longus origin outpaces its capacity to adapt. Each kick, side-step, reach or skating stride loads the adductor eccentrically at long length and transmits force across the anterior pubis. This happens through an aponeurotic connection with the contralateral rectus sheath, the symphysis capsule and the opposite adductor longus [r8]. Pain usually starts as stiffness after training and progresses to pain during sport, especially with sudden increases in match or training load [r4,r6].

name: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture
summary: A partial or complete tear of the ACL, usually from a non-contact deceleration, landing or cutting movement with the knee near extension and collapsing into valgus.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: 9–12 months after reconstruction; rehab-first pathway 3–6 months to stable function

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Not before 9 months post-reconstruction and only once criteria are met

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Lachman (Sn 85%, Sp 94%); pivot shift (Sp 98%)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI confirms and identifies associated meniscal, chondral and bone injuries

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 15–25 years

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: ~70% non-contact

grading: Anatomical sprain grade (with instrumented / clinical laxity)

structures: Lateral femoral condyle & posterolateral tibial plateau
keywords.mechanism: The classic non-contact ACL rupture happens about 40 ms after initial foot contact during a deceleration, side-step cut or one-leg landing. The knee is only slightly flexed (≈20–30°) and collapses into valgus coupled with internal tibial rotation while ground-reaction forces peak at about three times body weight [r3]. A strong quadriceps contraction near extension adds anterior tibial shear, which the ACL must resist [r2].

name: Articular cartilage (chondral/osteochondral) defect of the knee
populations: people after ACL injury or patellar dislocation
summary: A focal loss of articular (hyaline) cartilage, with or without underlying bone, from impaction, shear or chronic overload. It causes activity-related pain and effusion and has very limited capacity to heal.

keyFacts.label: Prevalence
keyFacts.value: Chondral lesions in ~60% of knee arthroscopies; full-thickness defects in 36% of athletes

keyFacts.label: Healing
keyFacts.value: Hyaline cartilage is avascular and has almost no intrinsic capacity to heal

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No accurate clinical test; MRI with cartilage-sensitive sequences or arthroscopy confirms

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI shows depth, size and subchondral bone; radiographs for loose bodies and alignment

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: 76% after cartilage surgery; ~5 months (OAT) to ~12 months (ACI)

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: 3-month active rehab trial first; 9–18 months after cartilage repair

grading: ICRS (International Cartilage Regeneration & Joint Preservation Society) grade

keywords.mechanism: Acute defects occur when high compressive load is combined with shear: a landing or pivot on a flexed knee, the femorotibial impaction of an ACL pivot-shift, the shear of a patella dislocating and relocating, or a direct blow on a flexed knee. Chronic defects develop when repetitive load exceeds the capacity of cartilage in a joint with malalignment, instability or meniscal loss. The weight-bearing medial femoral condyle and the patella are most often affected [r2,r3].

name: Degenerative meniscal tear
summary: A slowly developing meniscal lesion, usually a horizontal cleavage of the medial posterior horn in people over 35, often an early feature of osteoarthritis. Exercise therapy is first-line, not arthroscopy.

keyFacts.label: First-line care
keyFacts.value: Supervised exercise therapy and education for about 12 weeks

keyFacts.label: Arthroscopy
keyFacts.value: Partial meniscectomy is no better than sham surgery or exercise; not first-line

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Weight-bearing radiographs if needed; MRI is usually not indicated first-line

keyFacts.label: Prevalence
keyFacts.value: Present on MRI in 19–56% of people aged 50–90; most are asymptomatic

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Over 35 years; most common from 50 onwards

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Improvement over 3–6 months, continuing to 2 years

grading: MRI meniscal signal grade (intrasubstance to surface tear)

keywords.mechanism: There is no significant injury. With age and cumulative compressive load, the meniscal matrix loses its organisation and strength, so a trivial movement such as rising from a squat with a small twist is enough to complete a tear. Shear stress within the wedge produces a horizontal cleavage, most often in the posterior horn of the medial meniscus, where compressive load in flexion is greatest [r1,r10].

name: Femoral neck stress fracture
aka: fatigue fracture of the femoral neck
populations: female athletes with low energy availability
summary: A fatigue fracture of the femoral neck from repetitive loading, usually in runners and recruits. Tension-side fractures can displace and cause avascular necrosis, so suspected cases need urgent MRI.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Compression-side, low grade: about 6–14 weeks; after fixation: 3–6+ months

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Graded return to running once walking and hopping are pain-free and imaging shows healing

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No accurate clinical test; groin pain on hopping or weight-bearing should prompt MRI

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs often normal early; MRI is the definitive investigation

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 3% of sport-related stress fractures

keyFacts.label: Risk
keyFacts.value: High-risk site: delayed diagnosis increases displacement, AVN and career-ending outcomes

differentials: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
keywords.mechanism: With each foot strike, body weight and muscle forces bend the femoral neck in the frontal plane: the inferomedial cortex is compressed and the superolateral cortex is placed in tension. Thousands of submaximal loading cycles create microdamage faster than targeted remodelling can repair it, so bone resorption temporarily exceeds formation and the neck weakens [r2,r5]. Compression-side injuries begin at the inferomedial neck; tension-side injuries start superolaterally, where crack propagation and poor healing make displacement more likely [r4].

name: Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) syndrome
populations: male adolescent and young adult athletes
summary: Motion-related hip or groin pain caused by premature contact between the femur and acetabulum, from cam and/or pincer morphology, with positive clinical signs and imaging findings.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: At least 3 months of exercise-based care; 6–12 months after arthroscopy

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: FADIR: high sensitivity (≈94–99%), so a negative test helps rule out; it cannot confirm

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: AP pelvis + lateral (e.g. Dunn 45°) radiographs first; MRI/MRA only if it will change management

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Late adolescence to 40s; cam morphology forms before the growth plate closes

keyFacts.label: Diagnosis
keyFacts.value: Triad: symptoms + clinical signs + imaging (Warwick Agreement)

keyFacts.label: Management
keyFacts.value: Physio-led exercise first line; arthroscopy gives a modest extra short-term benefit in selected patients

differentials: Acetabular labral tear (without distinct bony morphology)
keywords.mechanism: FAI syndrome is a motion-driven overuse condition rather than a single injury. During hip flexion, especially when combined with adduction and internal rotation, a cam bump at the anterosuperior head–neck junction is levered into the acetabulum, or a pincer rim contacts the femoral neck early [r3,r12]. Repeated contact shears the acetabular cartilage away from the labrum (cam) or crushes the labrum between rim and neck (pincer). Symptoms appear when cumulative load exceeds the capacity of the chondrolabral tissues.

name: Hip (proximal femoral) fracture in older adults
populations: people with frailty, dementia or falls history
summary: A fracture of the femoral neck or trochanteric region, usually from a sideways fall onto the hip in an older adult with fragile bone. Treated with early surgery, mobilisation within 36 h and multidisciplinary rehab.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most mobility gains in 3–6 months; many never regain pre-fracture mobility

keyFacts.label: Key priority
keyFacts.value: Surgery within 24–48 h and mobilisation within 36 h of surgery

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: AP pelvis and lateral hip radiograph; MRI if clinical suspicion persists despite normal films

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean about 85 years; about 75% women

keyFacts.label: Mortality
keyFacts.value: Roughly 1 in 5 die within a year; 5–8× higher risk of death in the first 3 months

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Sideways fall with impact on the greater trochanter

structures: Soft tissues over the greater trochanter
differentials: Femoral neck stress or insufficiency fracture
Osteoporotic vertebral fracture with referred pain
Acetabular fracture or flare of hip osteoarthritis
keywords.mechanism: The typical hip fracture results from a fall directly sideways from standing height, with impact on the greater trochanter. In a prospective study of 206 consecutive hip fractures, 76% of patients fell directly to the side, 56% had a fresh haematoma over the greater trochanter, and most did not break the fall with an outstretched arm [r3]. The impact load through the trochanter bends and shears the femoral neck or trochanteric region, and osteoporotic bone fails at a load it would once have tolerated.

name: Inguinal-related groin pain ("sports hernia")
populations: kicking, sprinting and change-of-direction sport athletes
summary: Longstanding pain in the inguinal canal region with canal tenderness and no palpable hernia, typically worse with coughing, sneezing, sit-ups, sprinting and kicking. It is the Doha term for 'sports hernia'.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Rehabilitation-first for 6–12 weeks; ~73% return pain-free at about 10 weeks in rehab cohorts

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: After surgery for failed rehab, most return within 6–12 weeks

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Recognisable pain on inguinal canal palpation (scrotal invagination + Valsalva) and on resisted sit-up

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound (dynamic) to exclude true hernia; MRI for other entities

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mid-20s to early 30s (mean ~28 years in surgical series)

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Repetitive trunk rotation and hip extension under load: kicking, sprinting, cutting

tests: Inguinal canal palpation with Valsalva (scrotal invagination)
structures: External oblique aponeurosis and superficial ring
Ilioinguinal and genital branch of genitofemoral nerve
Adductor longus origin and rectus abdominis insertion
keywords.mechanism: IRGP is an overuse condition of the lower abdominal wall at the inguinal canal. Repetitive, forceful trunk rotation and hip extension during kicking, sprinting and cutting load the external oblique aponeurosis, the conjoint tendon and the transversalis fascia of the posterior inguinal wall. The rectus abdominis and abdominal wall pull the pubis upward while the adductors pull it downward. When this repetitive load exceeds tissue capacity, the posterior wall and aponeurosis attenuate and develop microtears, and the ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric or genitofemoral nerves can become irritated or entrapped [r3,r8].

name: Knee dislocation (multiligament knee injury)
populations: young adult males in high-energy trauma
summary: Disruption of two or more major knee ligaments, usually both cruciates, from high- or low-energy trauma. The knee may have spontaneously reduced; popliteal artery and peroneal nerve injury must be excluded.

keyFacts.label: Urgency
keyFacts.value: Emergency: limb-threatening popliteal artery injury in about 1 in 5

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Ankle–brachial index: <0.90 detected all arterial injuries in one prospective series

keyFacts.label: Nerve injury
keyFacts.value: Common peroneal nerve injury in about 25%

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: Schenck anatomic (KD-I to KD-V, with C and N modifiers)

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: 12–18 months; return to any sport about 54%, high-level sport 22–33%

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs, CT angiography if ABI <0.90 or abnormal pulses, then MRI

grading: Schenck anatomic classification of knee dislocation (Wascher modification)

keywords.mechanism: Dislocation needs disruption of most of the knee's restraints. High-energy mechanisms (vehicle crashes, falls from height) and sports collisions apply hyperextension, a posterior force on the flexed tibia, or combined varus/valgus with rotation. Hyperextension tends to produce anterior dislocation: the posterior capsule and PCL fail and the popliteal artery, tethered above and below the knee, is stretched. A dashboard blow to the flexed knee produces posterior dislocation, which has a high vascular injury rate [r2]. In people with obesity, a low-energy fall or misstep can dislocate the knee [r6].

name: Medial collateral ligament (MCL) sprain
summary: A sprain or tear of the medial collateral ligament from a valgus force, usually a blow to the outside of the knee. Most isolated tears, even complete ones, heal well with early functional rehabilitation.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Grade I ~2 weeks; grade II 3–4 weeks; grade III 6–8+ weeks

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Mean lay-off 23 days in professional football

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Valgus stress at 30° (pain and laxity together: LR+ 6.4 with history)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Usually clinical; MRI if laxity in extension or suspected ACL, meniscal or posteromedial injury

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: ~70% contact: a blow to the lateral knee

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Most common knee ligament injury in professional football

grading: Clinical grading (valgus stress at 30° flexion, opening compared with the other side)

tests: Valgus stress test in full extension
structures: Deep MCL and posterior oblique ligament
keywords.mechanism: The typical mechanism is a valgus force: a blow to the lateral side of the knee, or a fall or tackle onto it, with the foot planted and the knee slightly flexed (about 20–30°), where the superficial MCL is the dominant restraint [r1,r4]. External rotation of the tibia often accompanies the valgus load and adds stress to the deep MCL and posteromedial structures. Non-contact valgus-rotation injuries (cutting, skiing) also occur, and higher-energy or more extended-knee injuries may involve the ACL [r1].

name: Osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) of the knee
summary: A focal disorder of subchondral bone, usually on the lateral side of the medial femoral condyle in active adolescents, that can loosen the overlying cartilage and bone. Stable juvenile lesions often heal with offloading.

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 12–19 years; about 4 times more common in males

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 9.5 per 100,000 in 6–19-year-olds

keyFacts.label: Typical site
keyFacts.value: Medial femoral condyle (64%), classically its lateral aspect

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs including a notch (tunnel) view; MRI to assess size and stability

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Stable juvenile lesions: about two-thirds progress to healing in 6 months of offloading

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No reliable clinical test; diagnosis is radiological

grading: Stability and skeletal maturity, with the ROCK arthroscopic classification

keywords.mechanism: There is usually no single injury. Repetitive impact and shear load the subchondral bone of the femoral condyle faster than it can remodel, particularly in adolescents whose secondary ossification centre is still maturing. One theory is that the tibial spine impinges on the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle when the tibia rotates internally. The bone beneath the cartilage weakens, becomes ischaemic and separates from the parent bone, and the cartilage may then fissure and detach [r3].

name: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injury
populations: motor vehicle and motorcycle trauma patients
summary: A partial or complete tear of the PCL from a posteriorly directed force on the proximal tibia with the knee flexed, such as a dashboard impact or a fall onto a bent knee with the foot pointed.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Isolated grade I–II: usually back to sport within 2–3 months; reconstruction 9–12 months

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Dashboard impact (~35%) or fall on the flexed knee with foot plantarflexed (~24%)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Posterior drawer with tibial step-off (Sn 90%, Sp 99% in chronic isolated tears)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI for acute injury; posterior stress radiographs quantify laxity (>8 mm suggests complete tear, >12 mm combined injury)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mid-20s to early 30s

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Up to 38% of acute knee haemarthroses in trauma centres; mostly combined injuries

grading: Clinical grading of posterior laxity (posterior drawer at 90° flexion, tibial step-off)

tests: Dial test (tibial external rotation) at 30° and 90°
structures: Posterior cruciate ligament (anterolateral and posteromedial bundles)
Posterolateral corner (LCL, popliteus tendon, popliteofibular ligament)
keywords.mechanism: The classic mechanism is a posteriorly directed force on the anterior proximal tibia while the knee is flexed to about 90°. This happens when the tibia strikes the dashboard in a car crash, or when an athlete falls forward onto a flexed knee with the ankle plantarflexed so that the tibial tuberosity, rather than the patella, takes the impact [r3]. The tibia is driven backward in the sagittal plane and the PCL, which is tight in flexion, fails. Hyperflexion and hyperextension are less common mechanisms; hyperextension and varus-rotation mechanisms often injure the posterolateral corner as well [r1].

name: Posterolateral corner (LCL/PLC) injury
summary: Injury to the lateral collateral ligament, popliteus tendon and popliteofibular ligament from a varus, hyperextension or external rotation force. Usually combined with cruciate injury; easily missed.

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Varus stress at 0° and 30°; dial test at 30° and 90°

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI; varus stress radiographs (>4 mm side-to-side suggests grade III)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 9.1% of acute knee haemarthroses; 87% are combined injuries

keyFacts.label: Nerve risk
keyFacts.value: Common peroneal nerve injury in about one in four operated PLC injuries

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Grade I–II: 6–12 weeks; grade III reconstruction: 9–12 months

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Blow to the anteromedial knee in extension (hyperextension–varus)

grading: Clinical grading of varus/rotational laxity (with varus stress radiographs)

tests: Dial test (tibial external rotation at 30° and 90°)
structures: Medial femoral condyle and tibial plateau
keywords.mechanism: The classic mechanism is a posterolaterally directed blow to the anteromedial proximal tibia with the knee in or near full extension, which forces hyperextension and varus [r3]. Non-contact hyperextension–varus (landing or stepping awkwardly), and forced external rotation of the tibia on a flexed knee, also cause PLC injury. The force opens the lateral compartment in the frontal plane while the tibia rotates externally, and the medial compartment is compressed: an anteromedial femoral condyle bone bruise is a common MRI marker of this mechanism [r6].

name: Traumatic meniscal tear
populations: people with an acute ACL injury
manual workers who squat and twist
summary: An acute tear of the medial or lateral meniscus from twisting on a flexed, weight-bearing knee, causing joint-line pain, delayed swelling and sometimes catching or locking.

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Weight-bearing knee flexion with rotation on a planted foot

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Joint-line tenderness (Sn 83%, Sp 83%); Thessaly 20° (Sn 75%, Sp 87%)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI when surgery is being considered or the knee locks

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Mean ~2 months after partial meniscectomy; ~6 months after repair

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Exercise-first care: clinically relevant improvement by 12 weeks to 12 months

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adolescents and adults under 40 in pivoting sport

grading: Tear pattern and vascular zone (arthroscopic/MRI description)

keywords.mechanism: The classic non-contact mechanism is rotation of the femur on a fixed tibia while the knee is flexed and loaded, for example twisting to change direction with the foot planted. Axial compression traps the meniscus between the femoral condyle and tibial plateau while rotation and anteroposterior translation shear it. The posterior horn of the medial meniscus is least mobile and is the usual site; the lateral meniscus is more often torn at the time of an acute ACL rupture.
